entities.summary: Eucratides I, also known as Eucratides the Great, was a Greco-Bactrian king who ruled from approximately 170 BCE to 144 BCE. He was the son of Demetrius I and Stratonice, and succeeded his brother Demetrius II to the throne of Bactria. Eucratides expanded his empire, conquering much of northern India and extending Bactrian control to the Indus River. He also reformed the Bactrian currency, introducing a new coinage system that featured his own image and that of his predecessors. The reign of Eucratides I is notable for its cultural achievements, including the development of a distinctive Greco-Bactrian style of art and architecture, as well as his patronage of scholars and poets. His legacy endured for centuries, with his successors continuing to rule Bactria and his coinage being widely circulated throughout the ancient world. Eucratides I died in 144 BCE, and was succeeded by his son Euthydemus II, who went on to further expand Bactrian control in the region. The legacy of Eucratides I can be seen in the many archaeological sites that he founded or renovated, including the ancient city of Bactra, which remains one of the most important archaeological sites in the region today.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Eucratides I's reign was marked by significant cultural achievements, including the development of a distinctive Greco-Bactrian style of art and architecture. He also expanded Bactrian control to the Indus River and introduced a new coinage system that featured his own image and that of his predecessors.
